title: The Calibration Illusion
pitch: Single-file HTML toy recreating TabReliBench's core gotcha: a model's reliability diagram looks perfectly calibrated in aggregate while subgroup calibration is garbage. Simulate a sportsbook win-probability model split into bins the user controls via sliders (favorites vs dogs, home vs road, rest-advantage vs none). The overall calibration curve snaps to the 45-degree line no matter what, but a second panel shows subgroup curves fanning out wildly -- visualizing the paper's finding that 'rankings change a lot depending which axis you measure.' Punchline: this is why your backtest looked calibrated and still lost money on away dogs all season. Pure canvas/SVG + vanilla JS, no backend, buildable tonight.
discussion_why: Weaponizes a failure every sports/props bettor has lived -- model looks calibrated, bleeds money on a subset -- high relatability plus a 'wait, really?' surprise that aggregate calibration can mask total garbage, squarely in decision-theory/betting territory.

title: Laser Race: Beat AlphaEvolve's Omega
pitch: A single-file HTML 'golf' game where you manually tune block-partition parameters of a toy laser-method construction (tensor power slider, block-size choices, a few discrete combinatorial picks) and watch your implied matrix-multiplication exponent omega update live against a target line at the best known bound (~2.371339, as pushed by AlphaEvolve). A score bar shows your gap to the AI-found optimum; a reveal panel explains that an LLM-driven program search plus modern solvers beat decades of human hand-tuning on this exact combinatorial optimization. Hook: you're playing the same golf course AlphaEvolve played, and you will lose, visibly, in real time.
discussion_why: Less directly gambling-flavored but strong 'wait, really?' surprise (an LLM beat 50 years of math optimization on a famous open problem) and a playable human-vs-AI competitive frame that fits the games tag well; appeals more to the math/ai crowd than bettors.

title: Stopped Clock Judge: The AI That's Just Flipping Coins
pitch: Video built around CLM-as-a-Judge's finding that a cheap contrastive decision model scores statistically indistinguishable from a coin flip on RM-Bench/JudgeBench, and answers every single HaluEval item with one constant label -- yet looks fine on easy benchmarks. Frame it as a sports-betting-tout expose: run a live segment where a 'stopped clock' bot (always picks the favorite, or always says 'true') is scored against real LLM judges and real sports pundits on a mix of easy and hard prop questions. On easy slates the stopped clock looks like a genius; on hard ones it collapses to 50/50 -- exactly like a tout who only ever picks favorites. Close with: how do you tell a real edge from a broken clock that happens to be right twice a day? Cheap to storyboard, high shareability for a betting Discord that already distrusts touts.
discussion_why: Directly skewers the betting-tout archetype everyone in a sports/betting Discord has opinions about, strong 'wait, this AI judge is literally a coin flip?' surprise, and a built-in debate starter: how do you detect a broken-clock model before it costs you money.

title: Sinkhorn Speedrun: Watch Arbitrage-Free Odds Converge
pitch: Single-file HTML toy: two discrete price distributions (think implied win-probability histograms for a team at settlement vs. at an earlier checkpoint) sit on a canvas as draggable bar charts. Hit go and watch the Sinkhorn iterative-rescaling algorithm solve the martingale-constrained optimal-transport coupling live -- a heatmap matrix relaxing into place, paired with a log-scale error chart that the paper's exponential-convergence theorem predicts should be a straight line. A slider for the entropic regularization epsilon shows how fast/wiggly convergence is, and a 'break it' toggle removes the compact-support/convexity assumption so you can watch convergence stall. Framed as: this is the math that lets a sportsbook or options desk calibrate prices across time without creating free-money arbitrage -- directly relevant to why multi-leg parlay and futures pricing has to respect a martingale property.
discussion_why: Hits gambling/betting squarely (no-arbitrage pricing across time is exactly what futures/parlay markets must satisfy) with a genuine 'wait, exponential not just eventual?' surprise once the log-line snaps straight. Less whimsy, but strong decision-theory/math pull.

title: Beat the Bound: The Square-Root Near-Miss Challenge
pitch: Single HTML page: pick K>=8 square roots of distinct integers (default sqrt(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19)), then drag integer-coefficient sliders bounded by a max |c_i|<=H. The page instantly computes |sum c_i*sqrt(n_i)| and plots it on a log scale against the paper's explicit proven lower bound as a function of H -- a red floor line labeled 'provably impossible to get closer than this.' Users race to minimize the combination (local high-score table stored in localStorage) while the floor line mathematically guarantees they can never cross it, no matter how clever. A share-a-screenshot button turns each attempt into a 'how close I got to provably-impossible-zero' flex for the Discord.
discussion_why: Pure whimsy/math nerd-bait with a built-in competitive hook ('prove me wrong' challenges always get people grinding), plus a genuine surprise beat: a rigorous, explicit, provably-unbeatable number. Lower direct betting/poker tie-in than the others, but decision-theory/games framing (optimize against a hard bound) carries it.

title: Bracket Balance Auditor
pitch: Build a tool that takes any graph of matchups -- a poker league's head-to-head history, a fantasy draft pool, a tournament seeding bracket -- and applies the paper's explicit tight bound on how many edges can sit inside the union of any l of k balanced parts. Input a real partition (e.g. how your Discord split players into tables or divisions) and the tool flags whether the observed clustering of rivalries/rematches inside any subset of groups exceeds what's mathematically achievable under a truly balanced split, i.e. whether a bracket or table draw is 'suspiciously' imbalanced relative to the theoretical ceiling. Ships as a small web app: paste an edge list, pick k and l, get a verdict plus a visualization of the worst-case-vs-actual edge count.
discussion_why: Directly useful for seeding/table-balance arguments that already happen in poker nights and bracket pools ('the draw was rigged') and gives a hard mathematical referee for those debates -- solid games/sports fit, moderate surprise, but needs real implementation work so it's a slower burn than the demos.

title: PropSentiment: Granger-Causality Scanner for Niche Prop Markets
pitch: The paper finds investor sentiment (SENT, ARMS-style proxies) has weak memory but a real, testable Granger-causal relationship to returns on thin, frontier emerging markets -- exactly the regime that niche sports prop markets (WNBA, G-League, college, micro-markets at small books) resemble: low liquidity, slow information diffusion, retail-sentiment-driven line moves. Build a pipeline that scrapes social sentiment (Reddit/X volume + tone) around under-covered prop lines, runs the same Granger-style tests from the paper, and surfaces which markets show statistically significant sentiment-leads-line-movement structure before the number corrects -- a watchlist feed for bettors who want an edge in the long tail rather than the efficient major markets.
discussion_why: Dead-center betting/econ/decision-theory territory with an inherently arguable premise ('can sentiment really beat a niche market?') that invites exactly the kind of skeptical back-and-forth a betting Discord loves, plus the paper's own 'weak memory but real effect' finding is a built-in hedge for debate.

title: Steam or Sink
pitch: Single-file HTML toy based on the AMM/CEX optimal-execution paper: you've got a parent order to fill and must split your trading rate between a constant-function AMM pool (price moves along the bonding curve, visible slippage) and a lit CEX order book (visible depth, but a 'sharp detector' bot watching for footprint). A canvas chart shows both venue prices drifting as you drag two rate sliders each tick; a hidden detector score creeps up the more your flow looks non-random (mirrors how sportsbooks flag syndicate/steam money). Win condition: fill the order with minimal slippage AND stay under the detector threshold -- directly dramatizes the paper's 'hide order flow across venues' problem without needing its deep-learning solver (a square-root-law + inventory heuristic stands in).
discussion_why: Hitting on 'hiding your action from the book' is exactly what sharp bettors obsess over (line shopping, beard betting, structuring action to avoid limits) -- high relatability + decision-theory/gambling fit. The 'wait, crypto AMMs and sportsbooks have the same detection-evasion math' angle is a genuine surprise hook for a betting Discord.

title: Posterior-Mean Props: Full-Bayes Shrinkage for Early-Season Player Rates
pitch: Extends the existing nba-props edge-modeling terminal: the paper shows a fully Bayesian posterior-mean rule (vs. the classic NPMLE/empirical-Bayes estimator) can match the same sharp compound-decision risk bounds in a Gaussian setting. Build a shrinkage layer for small-sample player stats (e.g. 5-game 3PT% or rebound rate) that pools across the whole league's distribution instead of regressing each player toward a crude league average -- implement both the classic NPMLE and a Bayesian-nonparametric posterior-mean version side by side, backtest which produces tighter CLV on early-season player props where sample size is the whole problem.
discussion_why: Directly extends David's known nba-props edge work (memory: validated rebounds/threes under edges via GR-RTRMC), so it's concretely useful, not just theoretical -- strong buildable fit. Discussion-wise it's a genuine 'wait, you can shrink player stats without hand-picking a prior and get provably matching guarantees' surprise for a stats-literate betting crowd, though less whimsical/gambling-flavored than a pure demo.

title: Centipede Tilt
pitch: Single-file HTML/canvas toy riffing on the centipede locomotion model's core question: is the undulating body wave actively muscle-driven, or just passively resisted by leg-ground contact? Render a simple N-segment centipede; two sliders control 'stepping rate' and 'lateral stiffness' exactly like the paper's parameter sweep, and a toggle switches the body between 'active' (muscle-driven wave) and 'passive' (just along for the ride) mode so you can watch the same stepping rate produce wildly different gaits. Framed for the Discord as a tilt metaphor: are YOUR stake-size swings after a bad beat actively willed, or just passive momentum carrying you along -- drag the stiffness slider until the centipede (or your bankroll) falls over.
discussion_why: Pure whimsy payoff (bio/physics nerd-snipe, a wiggly centipede toy nobody expects on a betting server) plus a genuinely debatable framing -- 'is tilt active or passive' is the kind of half-joking, half-real argument that gets legs in a poker/sports chat. Lower direct betting-math fit than the other two, carried by surprise and delight.

title: The Empirical Bayes Showdown: Can a Full Bayesian Beat 60 Years of Math?
pitch: A 10-minute explainer walking through the compound-decision problem using a betting-native example: you're simultaneously estimating 'true skill' for hundreds of bettors or players at once from noisy small samples (think: grading 300 Discord cappers off 20 picks each). Visualize the classic NPMLE empirical-Bayes rule (Robbins' problem lineage) against the paper's fully Bayesian posterior-mean rule, animate both converging to the same sharp minimax risk bound as sample size grows, and end on the punchline: the 'more principled' full-Bayes approach doesn't need the two-step plug-in NPMLE at all and still provably ties it.
discussion_why: Niche statistical-theory content, but reframed around 'grading cappers off small samples' it's directly relevant to an argument every betting Discord has (is that guy actually good or just on a heater) -- moderate surprise ('wait, two totally different-looking estimators are provably the same?'), solid math/decision-theory fit, less inherently shareable than the demos.

title: Extinction Roulette: Your Bankroll's Hidden R0
pitch: The rabies paper's punchline: a branching-process/CTMC model has an explicit stochastic extinction threshold the deterministic ODE mean-field model can't see -- the mean trajectory can climb while most individual realizations go extinct. Port that exact math to a betting syndicate: model bankroll units as a birth-death CTMC where 'birth' = wins, 'death' = losses, tuned by edge/bet size (the R0 analog). Single HTML+canvas page: user sets edge and bet size, it draws the smooth deterministic mean curve climbing confidently, then fires 200 real stochastic sample paths underneath plus a live 'fraction already busted' counter that keeps climbing even with positive EV. The gap between the clean mean line and the messy, often-zero paths is the paper's thesis, felt in real time.
discussion_why: Weaponizes the classic bankroll-ruin debate ('but the EV is positive!') with a genuine 'wait, really?' result borrowed from epidemiology -- high relatability and dead-center fit for betting/decision-theory, plus whimsy in repurposing a disease-extinction model for degenerate parlay math.

title: One-Pass Hand Mutagenesis Scanner
pitch: The protein paper's core trick: instead of masking each residue one at a time across N forward passes, pseudo-perplexity scores every position's mutation in a single pass. Rebuild that batch-vs-iterative insight as a poker toy: take a 5-card hand and in one simulated 'pass' compute the equity delta of swapping every card to every other rank/suit, rendering a 5x51 heatmap -- which single-card mutation helps your hand's 'fitness' most, and which wreck it. Side-by-side timer showing the naive iterative approach (51 separate re-evaluations) crawling versus the one-pass scan finishing instantly makes the speedup itself the show.
discussion_why: Poker crowd loves hand-equity tooling and the 'score everything at once' trick is a genuine surprise lifted straight from a bio paper -- solid poker/math fit, moderate debate fuel (people will argue about the equity heuristic used), light AI angle.

title: Self-Healing Swarm: Bloch-Memory Boids
pitch: The paper gives flocking agents a bounded 'Bloch-type' internal memory vector (borrowed from qubit/spin dynamics) coupled to a slow regulatory state, letting the swarm recover coordination after a disruption instead of just reacting moment-to-moment. Build a canvas boids sim with two populations side by side: classic reactive boids vs. boids carrying a decaying, magnitude-bounded memory vector. Inject the same disruption into both (a predator dash scattering everyone) -- the memory-less swarm stays chaotic, the Bloch-memory swarm visibly 're-coheres' into formation within seconds. A slider exposes memory decay rate so you can watch the self-healing speed change live.
discussion_why: Visually striking and whimsical (qubit math driving pigeon-like flocking), with a loose but real analog to 'team chemistry/momentum after a disruption' debates sports fans already have -- strong whimsy and games fit, softer direct betting tie.

title: Reading Through the Lid: What Poker Tells Could Learn From Raman Spectroscopy
pitch: The Raman paper identifies bacteria -- down to distinguishing near-identical E. coli strains -- straight through an unopened, inverted agar plate lid, no sample prep, mid-incubation. A faceless explainer video builds the hook 'scientists can ID what's inside a sealed container without opening it' and runs it into poker: why can't we 'spectroscopically' read a hand through the felt? Walk through real non-invasive sensing (thermal, RF, vibration-based tell detection used in anti-cheat tech for live poker) and land on why true 'x-ray the hole cards' tech stays science fiction -- using the Raman result as the credible, genuinely surprising anchor that makes the comparison land instead of feeling like clickbait.
discussion_why: Strong 'wait, really?' hook (ID through a sealed, unopened lid) and a fun whimsical bridge to poker tells/cheating-detection, but the betting/poker tie is more narrative than mechanical so debate fuel is moderate rather than core.

title: Fade The Public: The Contrarian Phase Transition
pitch: Single-file HTML toy that reifies the paper's exact group-of-3 update equation for ratio-dependent contrarian activation. Instead of a fixed probability of flipping, each discussion group's contrarians activate as a function of the local majority/minority ratio r = n_maj/n_min. Sliders control the public's starting lean and the 'contrarian sensitivity' to r; a live bifurcation plot shows the vote-share fixed points split as sensitivity crosses the paper's derived critical threshold -- i.e. the exact moment 'fading the public' stops being noise and becomes a self-reinforcing reversal. Canvas renders the iterated map frame-by-frame so you can watch a 70/30 public lean either settle into a stable consensus or flip the other way depending on one slider.
discussion_why: Directly maps a 'do contrarians overreact or correctly call the top' debate every bettor has had about fading the public/line movement onto a real phase-transition math result -- surprising that there's an exact closed form, strong betting/decision-theory fit, and the bifurcation flip is a fun 'wait, really?' moment to argue about on Discord.

title: The Squeeze Illusion: Why Sharpening Your Model's Confidence Lies to You
pitch: A toy HTML demo built around the paper's core finding: MCMC/SMC samplers that claim to draw from a 'power distribution' p^alpha (the standard trick for sharpening a model's output confidence 'for free') actually fail to converge to that target. Render a simple bimodal toy distribution over two betting outcomes, let the user crank a temperature/alpha slider meant to sharpen it, and run a simplified resampling scheme live in-browser. Overlay the true p^alpha curve against what the sampler actually converges to -- the gap visibly grows as alpha increases, showing the 'free sharpening' is an illusion. Framed for anyone who temperature-scales a predictive model's win probabilities to size bets more aggressively: you're not getting more signal, you're getting a silently biased number.
discussion_why: Hits quant bettors/poker solvers directly in a sore spot -- everyone who temperature-scales a model's confidence for bet sizing will recognize the move, and the 'the sharpening you thought was free is actually broken' result is a genuine surprise worth arguing about, though it's a notch nerdier/less visceral than a straight betting-market analogy.

title: Explainable Steam: Local Diagnostics for Line-Movement Anomalies
pitch: Port the HL-LHC paper's trick -- local diagnostics that recover why a flagged event is anomalous in a learned embedding space, not just that it is -- onto sports betting line/odds data. Build a small embedding model over line-movement feature vectors (odds velocity, book divergence, bet-ticket vs money %), flag anomalies ('steam') the way the physicists flag rare collision events, then attach the paper's local-diagnostic layer so each flagged steam move comes with a feature-attribution readout: 'this move is anomalous mainly because of book divergence, not bet-count skew.' Natural extension of SharpLab's existing CLV tracking -- turns a black-box anomaly flag into a receipt a bettor can actually act on.
discussion_why: Sharp-money detection with an actual 'show your work' layer is catnip for the betting crowd -- it answers the perennial 'is this really steam or just noise' argument with attributable evidence instead of vibes, strong fit even if it reads more like infrastructure than spectacle.

title: Platonic Poker: Does Hand Strength Live in a Shared Abstract Space?
pitch: The paper's theory says multilingual LLMs converge on near-identical inner representations because the underlying data shares a hidden hierarchical grammar -- abstract levels shared across languages, surface levels language-specific. Test the poker analogue: train (or probe an existing) hand-strength encoder across different poker variants (hold'em, PLO, short-deck) which share abstract strategic structure (equity, nut potential, range pressure) but differ wildly in surface rules (4 hole cards vs 2, different deck). Project aims to show a 'platonic hand-strength axis' emerging independent of variant -- i.e. two hands from different games that are 'the same abstract hand' cluster together in embedding space even though their raw card representations look nothing alike.
discussion_why: A genuinely fun 'is there a universal poker intuition underneath all these different games' question that poker players will have opinions on, though it's a longer research build than a Discord-night spark and the payoff needs real training/eval work to land.

title: The Gambler's Exit Clock
pitch: Single-file HTML toy built around the paper's core object: a 'first-exit-time functional' — will a stochastic process leave a safe region before time T? The paper's contribution is showing that cheap/crude numerical approximations of this functional systematically mis-estimate exit risk, which is dangerous when it's feeding a safety-critical controller. Reframe the 'safe region' as your bankroll staying above zero, and T as a session length or a betting day. User sets edge, variance, and bankroll, then drags a slider between 'crude discretization' and the paper's higher-order approximation, watching the computed bust-probability-before-T visibly shift — same process, same inputs, different answer depending on how carefully you integrate the exit time. The hook: this is literally gambler's ruin, but with a rigorous lesson about why naive Monte Carlo risk tools quietly lie to you about how close you are to blowing up.
discussion_why: Bankroll ruin is core gambling canon, so everyone has priors to argue with; the 'your risk calculator is wrong and here's the math for why' angle is a genuine surprise hook, and it fits decision-theory/gambling tags cleanly without forcing it.

title: Dictator or Decoy?
pitch: The Courtade-Kumar stability result says: if a Boolean (yes/no) function's 'information' is close to the maximum possible, the function itself must be probabilistically close to a dictator function — one where a single input variable decides the whole output, full stop. Build a toy where the user assembles a 'betting signal' as a Boolean function of 4-6 binary inputs (line moved, star player out, home dog, back-to-back, revenge game, public is heavy on one side) via a small interactive truth table or sliders. The demo computes the function's information content live, plots it against the extremal dictator value, and — when it's close — reveals the sharp stability bound on how close your fancy multi-factor function actually is to just being 'if X then bet, else don't,' with X highlighted. Built-in gut-punch mode: load a few real stereotypical handicapper rules and watch most of them collapse onto one dominant variable.
discussion_why: Directly weaponizable against anyone's '10-factor model' in a betting Discord — it's relatable (everyone has a pet multi-stat system), surprising (a real theorem says complexity often collapses to one variable), and the word 'dictator function' is just inherently funny to drop into a sports chat.

title: Hit-and-Run GTO Race
pitch: The paper proves a sharp spectral-gap (mixing-speed) bound for the Hit-and-Run walk sampling a convex body, tied to the body's Poincare constant, and does the same for its axis-aligned cousin Coordinate Hit-and-Run. Render a mixed-strategy simplex (e.g. a 3-action bluff/check/raise frequency triangle, or a river bet-sizing range) as the convex body, then animate both samplers taking random steps inside it simultaneously, side by side, with a live histogram showing how fast each one forgets its starting corner and converges to uniform coverage. Let the user stretch the simplex into a narrow sliver (an elongated range that's heavily skewed toward one action) and watch Coordinate Hit-and-Run visibly choke while full Hit-and-Run barely slows down — a direct, visual demonstration of the paper's degree/shape-dependent mixing gap.
discussion_why: Strong poker/GTO crowd appeal and a genuine 'wait, one sampler just breaks on skewed ranges' surprise, but it's more niche to solver-heads than to a general betting audience, so slightly lower broad discussion pull.

title: I Let GPT-5.6 Prove the Theorem, Then Bet on Whether It Mixes
pitch: The paper proves a degree-free spectral independence bound for Holant measures — the statistical-physics framework covering monomer-dimer models (think domino tilings) and b-matchings — guaranteeing Glauber dynamics mixes fast even on high-degree graphs. The authors note the key proof ideas came from GPT-5.6. Video concept: open with a physical domino-tiling puzzle on a grid, explain monomer-dimer coverings as a 'matching game,' then run a live Glauber-dynamics sampler on screen that randomly flips tile pairs toward a uniform random tiling — and let viewers bet (via poll/chat) on whether it converges within N steps on a nasty high-degree graph before revealing the theorem that guarantees it will. The real hook is the meta-bit: cut to the actual proof sketch and discuss, soberly, what it means that an AI supplied the core argument — a mini debate on trusting AI-generated math, dressed as a parlor game about tiling puzzles.
discussion_why: Combines a genuinely weird-and-delightful game (domino tiling as gambling fodder) with the 'AI proved real math' surprise that reliably triggers debate about AI capability/trust — good whimsy plus an AI-skeptic-vs-booster flashpoint for the server.
